section.title: Peter and Cornelius
section.sectionRationale: As Peter heals Aeneas and raises Dorcas, God prepares him for a far greater work. Through matching visions, a Roman centurion in Caesarea and the apostle Peter are drawn together, God teaches Peter to call no person unclean, and while Peter preaches, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles just as at Pentecost. When the circumcised believers object, Peter recounts it all in Jerusalem, and the church glorifies God that He has granted repentance and life even to the Gentiles. This is the door to the nations opened by God Himself.
section.thesis: God sovereignly opens the gospel to the Gentiles, teaching Peter and the church that He shows no favoritism but pours out His Spirit on all who believe, so that the once-for-all door to the nations is thrown open and the mission of the risen Christ reaches beyond Israel to the whole world.
section.frameNote: Six movements: Peter heals Aeneas and raises Dorcas; Cornelius's vision in Caesarea; Peter's vision of the sheet in Joppa; Peter enters a Gentile house; Peter preaches and the Spirit falls on the Gentiles; and Peter defends the whole event before the church in Jerusalem.

units.label: Peter heals Aeneas and raises Dorcas
units.note: signs that turn many to the Lord

verses.text: As Peter traveled throughout the area, he went to visit the saints in Lydda.
There he found a man named Aeneas who had been paralyzed and bedridden for eight years.
“Aeneas,” Peter said to him, “Jesus Christ heals you! Get up and put away your mat.” Immediately Aeneas got up,
and all who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.
In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (which is translated as Dorcas), who was always occupied with works of kindness and charity.
At that time, however, she became sick and died, and her body was washed and placed in an upper room.
Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to urge him, “Come to us without delay.”

So Peter got up and went with them. On his arrival, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood around him, weeping and showing him the tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was still with them.
Then Peter sent them all out of the room. He knelt down and prayed, and turning toward her body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and seeing Peter, she sat up.
Peter took her by the hand and helped her up. Then he called the saints and widows and presented her to them alive.
This became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord.
And Peter stayed for several days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon.

units.label: Cornelius's vision
units.note: a God-fearing centurion is told to send for Peter

verses.text: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion in what was called the Italian Regiment.
He and all his household were devout and God-fearing. He gave generously to the people and prayed to God regularly.
One day at about the ninth hour, he had a clear vision of an angel of God who came to him and said, “Cornelius!”
Cornelius stared at him in fear and asked, “What is it, Lord?” The angel answered, “Your prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God.
Now send men to Joppa to call for a man named Simon who is called Peter.
He is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea.”
When the angel who spoke to him had gone, Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among his attendants.
He explained what had happened and sent them to Joppa.

units.label: Peter's vision of the sheet
units.note: do not call unclean what God has made clean

verses.text: The next day at about the sixth hour, as the men were approaching the city on their journey, Peter went up on the roof to pray.
He became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven open and something like a large sheet being let down to earth by its four corners.
It contained all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, as well as birds of the air.
Then a voice said to him: “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!”
“No, Lord!” Peter answered. “I have never eaten anything {{koinos|impure}} or unclean.”
The voice spoke to him a second time: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.”
This happened three times, and all at once the sheet was taken back up into heaven.

units.label: Peter enters a Gentile house
units.note: God has shown me to call no man unclean

verses.text: While Peter was puzzling over the meaning of the vision, the men sent by Cornelius found Simon’s house and approached the gate.
They called out to ask if Simon called Peter was staying there.
As Peter continued to reflect on the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you.
So get up! Go downstairs and accompany them without hesitation, because I have sent them.”
So Peter went down to the men and said, “Here am I, the one you are looking for. Why have you come?”

“Cornelius the centurion has sent us,” they said. “He is a righteous and God-fearing man with a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation. A holy angel instructed him to request your presence in his home so he could hear a message from you.”
So Peter invited them in as his guests. And the next day he got ready and went with them, accompanied by some of the brothers from Joppa.
The following day he arrived in Caesarea, where Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.
As Peter was about to enter, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet to worship him.
But Peter helped him up. “Stand up,” he said, “I am only a man myself.”
As Peter talked with him, he went inside and found many people gathered together.
He said to them, “You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him. But God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean.
So when I was invited, I came without objection. I ask, then, why have you sent for me?”
Cornelius answered: “Four days ago I was in my house praying at this, the ninth hour. Suddenly a man in radiant clothing stood before me
and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your gifts to the poor have been remembered before God.
Therefore send to Joppa for Simon, who is called Peter. He is a guest in the home of Simon the tanner, by the sea.’
So I sent for you immediately, and you were kind enough to come. Now then, we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has instructed you to tell us.”

units.label: Peter preaches and the Spirit falls on the Gentiles
units.note: God shows no favoritism, and the gift is poured out on the nations

verses.text: Then Peter began to speak: “I now truly understand that God does not show {{prosopolemptes|favoritism}},
but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right.
He has sent this message to the people of Israel, proclaiming the gospel of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.
You yourselves know what has happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee with the baptism that John proclaimed:
how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and how Jesus went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with Him.
We are witnesses of all that He did, both in the land of the Jews and in Jerusalem. And although they put Him to death by hanging Him on a tree,
God raised Him up on the third day and caused Him to be seen,
not by all the people, but by the witnesses God had chosen beforehand, by us who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead.
And He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that He is the One appointed by God to judge the living and the dead.
All the prophets testify about Him that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name.”
While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard his message.
All the circumcised believers who had accompanied Peter were astounded that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been {{ekcheo|poured out}} even on the {{ethnos|Gentiles}}.
For they heard them speaking in tongues and exalting God. Then Peter said,
“Can anyone withhold the water to baptize these people? They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have!”
So he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay for a few days.

units.label: Peter defends it in Jerusalem
units.note: God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life

verses.text: The apostles and brothers throughout Judea soon heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God.
So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers took issue with him
and said, “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them.”
But Peter began and explained to them the whole sequence of events:
“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision of something like a large sheet being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came right down to me.
I looked at it closely and saw four-footed animals of the earth, wild beasts, reptiles, and birds of the air.
Then I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter, kill and eat.’
‘No, Lord,’ I said, ‘for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’
But the voice spoke from heaven a second time, ‘Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.’
This happened three times, and everything was drawn back up into heaven.
Just then three men sent to me from Caesarea stopped at the house where I was staying.
The Spirit told me to accompany them without hesitation. These six brothers also went with me, and we entered the man’s home.
He told us how he had seen an angel standing in his house and saying, ‘Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter.
He will convey to you a message by which you and all your household will be saved.’
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning.
Then I remembered the word of the Lord, how He said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’
So if God gave them the same gift He gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to hinder the work of God?”
When they heard this, they had no further objections, and they glorified God, saying, “So then, God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life.”

koinos.gloss: Common, ordinary, and so ritually impure or defiled. Peter's refusal, I have never eaten anything common, reflects the food laws that fenced Israel off from the nations. God's word, do not call common what I have made clean, reaches past food to people, tearing down the wall between Jew and Gentile.

prosopolemptes.gloss: One who shows partiality or accepts persons by outward appearance. Peter confesses that God is not such a One; He plays no favorites among the nations but welcomes all who fear Him and turn to Christ, the truth that unlocks the Gentile mission.

ekcheo.gloss: To pour out, to shed abroad. The same word describes the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost, now poured out on Gentiles, showing that God has given them the identical gift and made no second-class members in His church.

ethnos.gloss: A nation or people; in the plural, the Gentiles, the nations outside Israel. That the gift falls on the ethne is the astonishment of the circumcised believers and the hinge of the whole episode, the door of the gospel thrown open to the world.

basic.context: Peter is on a healing tour, restoring Aeneas and raising Dorcas, when God sets up a much larger work. A devout Roman officer named Cornelius is told by an angel to send for Peter. Meanwhile Peter sees a vision of a sheet full of unclean animals and hears God say not to call unclean what He has made clean. The two men meet, Peter preaches Christ, and the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles as they listen. Back in Jerusalem some object that Peter ate with the uncircumcised, but when he tells the story they praise God. The key questions are: what does the sheet vision really mean, why does the Spirit fall as it does, and is this a pattern or a one-time opening of the door.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the whole long section as one connected argument that God, not Peter, opens the gospel to the Gentiles. The sheet vision is about people, not diet, as Peter himself explains in verse 28. The falling of the Spirit before baptism is God's public seal that Gentiles are received on the same terms as Jews. The Jerusalem debate shows the church learning to bow to what God has plainly done.
basic.originalLanguages: Peter will not eat what is koinos, common or unclean, until God overturns the whole category. He then confesses that God is no prosopolemptes, no shower of favoritism. When the Spirit is ekcheo, poured out, on the ethne, the Gentiles, the same gift given at Pentecost, the matter is settled. The words carry the story from the wall of separation to its fall.
basic.typology: Peter's raising of Dorcas echoes Jesus raising the dead and points to the resurrection life the gospel brings. The clean and unclean animals fulfil and then retire the food laws that had pictured Israel's separateness. This Gentile Pentecost answers the Babel scattering, gathering the nations by the one Spirit.
basic.christ: Peter's sermon is the centre: Jesus of Nazareth anointed with the Spirit, doing good, crucified on a tree, raised on the third day, appointed judge, and the one through whose name everyone who believes receives forgiveness. It is while this Christ is preached that the Spirit falls. The door to the nations opens only because Christ is Lord of all.
basic.god: God directs every step: the visions, the timing, the command to go, and the outpouring of the Spirit. He shows no favoritism, welcomes those from every nation, and grants even the Gentiles repentance unto life. The whole episode magnifies God's initiative; the church can only recognise and rejoice in what He has done.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 2 is the Pentecost this outpouring matches. Acts 15 settles the question this event raised, that Gentiles are saved by grace apart from the law. Galatians 2 recalls the ongoing struggle over eating with Gentiles. Ephesians 2 celebrates the wall of hostility torn down.
basic.oneStory: This is the door to the nations opened by God's own hand. The promise that in Abraham all peoples would be blessed reaches a decisive fulfilment as the Spirit falls on a Gentile household. From here the gospel is unmistakably for the world, and the church can never again treat any nation as unclean.

context.literary:
This is the longest continuous narrative in Acts so far, running from 9:32 to 11:18, and its length is itself a statement. Luke tells the story of Cornelius in full in chapter 10, then lets Peter tell it again in 11:4-17, and Peter will recall it once more at the Jerusalem council, 15:7-11. An event told three times is an event Luke wants fixed in the reader's mind.

The unit is built in three movements around two visions. Peter's two miracles at Lydda and Joppa, 9:32-43, bring him to the coast and settle him in the house of Simon the tanner. Then comes the long double scene: a vision to Cornelius, 10:1-8, matched by a vision to Peter, 10:9-16, and the two sets of messengers meet at the gate, 10:17-23. The two halves of the double vision are carefully balanced in the number of times and the time of day: ninth hour, sixth hour, three times, three men. Finally the meeting itself, 10:24-48, and the defence in Jerusalem, 11:1-18.

The story is full of reversals. A Roman centurion, an officer of the occupying army, is the one who prays and gives to the poor, while the apostle is the one who must be taught. Peter's own words show it. He enters and says 'I am only a man myself,' 10:26, to the soldier who falls at his feet, and his sermon begins with the confession that he has just understood something, 10:34. The apostle is the learner and the Gentile is the one whom heaven visits first.

Notice also how the narrator manages interruption. Peter is 'still speaking' when the Spirit falls, 10:44, and the sermon never reaches its planned end. God stops the preacher mid-sentence, and the retelling in 11:15 says the Spirit fell 'as I began to speak.' The Spirit's timing is part of the argument.

The final verse of the unit, 11:18, is the response of a church: they fall silent, then glorify God. Luke gives the last word to the praise of the people who had come to argue.
context.historical:
Peter's two miracles take place on the coastal plain. Lydda lay inland and Joppa was the port on the old Philistine coast, and the two were near enough that the disciples could send for him, 9:38. The name Aeneas is Greek, and Tabitha's Aramaic name means a gazelle, as does the Greek Dorcas, names that hint at a mixed population among whom the church had already taken root. Peter's host Simon was a tanner, a trade that handled the skins of dead animals and that many strict Jews regarded as ritually unclean. Peter is therefore already lodging in a house that stood a little outside the circle of strict purity before the vision comes to him.

Caesarea was the Roman administrative capital of Judea, a port city built by Herod the Great and named for the emperor. Cornelius is a centurion, commanding about a hundred men, in a cohort named the Italian. He is described as 'devout and God-fearing,' 10:2, a person who worshipped the God of Israel and supported the synagogue without having been circumcised. Luke uses similar language of Gentiles who attended Jewish worship elsewhere, for example Acts 13:16. Such people stood at the edge of the community, welcomed to listen and to pray but not fully inside.

The wall between Jew and Gentile was one of custom and purity more than of statute. The Law forbade eating unclean animals, Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14, and a Jew's strictness about food made shared meals with Gentiles hard. Peter calls it 'unlawful,' 10:28, though no verse of the Law forbids visiting a Gentile; he is speaking of the accepted rule of his people. Even the Jewish leaders who brought Jesus to Pilate would not enter the Praetorium, to avoid being defiled, John 18:28. It is precisely this habit that the vision overthrows, and the critics in 11:3 are objecting to the table, not to the preaching.

Joppa has one more association that Luke leaves unspoken. It was from Joppa that Jonah set out in flight from God's command to take His word to a Gentile city, Jonah 1:3. Peter goes from Joppa to Caesarea in obedience, though still reluctant.
context.canonical:
The promise that the nations would be blessed is as old as Abraham, Genesis 12:3, and the prophets sharpened it: the Servant would be a light to the nations, Isaiah 49:6, and the foreigner who joined himself to the LORD would be brought to His holy mountain, Isaiah 56:6-8. Luke has been carrying that promise through Acts. The risen Lord had said that repentance and forgiveness would be proclaimed to all nations, Luke 24:47, and Acts 1:8 had set out the plan. Samaria in chapter 8 and the Ethiopian were the first steps; this is the decisive one.

The Spirit's falling is tied back to Pentecost twice. Peter says it fell 'just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning,' 11:15, and he remembers the Lord's words of Acts 1:5, 'you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit,' 11:16. At the Jerusalem council he will say that God made no distinction, cleansing their hearts by faith, 15:7-11, and James will quote Amos 9:11-12 about the nations bearing the LORD's name, 15:14-17.

Paul's letters give the doctrine that rests on the event: there is no difference between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is Lord of all, Romans 10:12, and in Christ the dividing wall of hostility has been torn down, Ephesians 2:13-18. Galatians 2:11-14 shows that the lesson was not learned painlessly: even Peter later drew back from eating with Gentiles at Antioch, and Paul had to oppose him. The story of Cornelius is therefore both a settled foundation and a reminder of how easily the church forgets it.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers, many of them Gentiles, to know that their place in the people of God is not an accident or a concession. It was planned, announced and carried out by God. Every element of the story serves that: the angel to Cornelius, the vision to Peter, the Spirit's explicit instruction, the six Jewish brothers who go along as witnesses, and the telling of the story to the Jerusalem church. By the end no one can say the Gentiles were let in by a human decision, and no one can say that Peter acted alone.

He also wants to show how the church comes to see a new thing. They do not decide in advance; they follow what God has done. Peter reasons from the gift of the Spirit to the baptism, 10:47, and the church reasons from Peter's report to praise, 11:18. The Scriptures will be brought in at Acts 15, but the sequence is clear: God acts, the church recognises, and then the Scriptures are understood in a new light.

Luke finally means to honour Cornelius without making him a hero. He is a prayerful, generous man whom God notices, and he is also a man who needs to hear a message by which he will be saved, 11:14. The story holds both: God's attention reaches those who seek Him, and the message of Christ is still what saves.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The sheet vision and its application are recorded as history. Peter's meal habits changed, and the church's practice of table fellowship across the Jew and Gentile line is now a matter of settled apostolic teaching, but the narrative does not itself legislate. The settled rule comes in Acts 15 and in the letters, where Gentile believers are received without circumcision and the old barrier is taken down.

The pattern of the Spirit falling before baptism is not a command about the order of baptism and the Spirit. Luke tells us what happened here, and the order differs elsewhere in Acts, for example 2:38 and 8:16-17. What is normative is Peter's reasoning that those who have received the Spirit have plainly been accepted by God and must not be kept from the water.

The command not to call anything impure is not a licence to ignore all moral categories. God cleansed what He had made, the people and the food, but the same chapter praises a man who 'does what is right,' 10:35. Cleansing does not abolish righteousness; it removes the ethnic and ceremonial barrier that stood between people and the God who welcomes them.

debates.question: Does the vision of the sheet declare all foods clean, or is it only about people?

views.label: It is about people, with food as the vehicle
views.case: Peter himself gives the meaning twice: 'God has shown me that I should not call any man impure or unclean,' 10:28, and in 10:34 he says that God shows no favouritism. The animals are the picture and the Gentiles are the point. The matter at issue in Jerusalem, 11:3, was eating with uncircumcised men, not menus.

views.label: It is about both, since the food laws were what kept Jew and Gentile apart
views.case: The voice speaks of animals, and Peter protests about food, 10:14. The Law's distinction between clean and unclean animals was the practical mark of Israel's separateness, Leviticus 20:24-26. Mark's remark that Jesus declared all foods clean, Mark 7:19, shows the Lord had already begun the change. The vision removes the practical wall, and then the people come through the door.

debates.bearing: Either way the apostle's own application is to people, and the church acts on it. The disagreement concerns whether the food laws themselves were also set aside here, and the later texts, Acts 15 and Galatians 2, treat the barrier to table fellowship as finished.

debates.question: Was Cornelius already saved before Peter came?

views.label: He was already a believer in the God of Israel and needed the fuller word
views.case: The angel says his prayers and gifts have ascended as a memorial before God, 10:4, and Peter says God welcomes those who fear Him and do what is right, 10:35. On this reading Cornelius was like an Old Testament believer, accepted by faith in the promises, and he now enters the fullness of the new age through Christ and the Spirit.

views.label: He was not yet saved, though God was drawing him
views.case: The angel does not tell him he is saved but tells him to send for a man who will speak words by which he and all his household 'will be saved,' 11:14. Peter's sermon ends with forgiveness through Jesus' name for everyone who believes in Him, 10:43, and the church's conclusion is that God has granted the Gentiles repentance unto life, 11:18. No one is saved apart from Christ, Acts 4:12.

views.label: God was working on him by grace before the gospel reached him, and the sermon is the means of salvation
views.case: A mediating view holds that his fear of God, prayer and generosity are themselves the fruit of God's prior work, not its cause. The sequence is God's initiative from first to last: a prompting, a vision, a messenger, a message, faith, and the Spirit. This respects both the praise of his devotion and the necessity of the message.

debates.bearing: The story lets us honour Cornelius's seeking and insist on Christ at once. The fact that God sent an angel and an apostle shows how seriously He takes the message that saves.

debates.question: Is the Gentile Pentecost a pattern for every believer?

views.label: It is a unique, once-for-all opening of the door
views.case: Peter calls it 'the same gift' given 'at the beginning,' 11:15-17, and treats it as a stage in salvation history: Jews, Samaritans, Gentiles. After it, the church takes the Gentile mission as settled and the later chapters do not repeat the pattern.

views.label: It shows what normally happens when anyone believes
views.case: The Spirit falls as people hear and believe, apart from any rite or laying on of hands, 10:44. Peter says everyone who believes in Jesus' name receives forgiveness, 10:43, and later Paul says that all who belong to Christ have the Spirit, Romans 8:9. The speaking in tongues here is a sign for the circumcised who needed convincing, but the reception of the Spirit at faith is the normal pattern.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the Spirit is the seal of God's acceptance. They differ on how much of the visible sign should be expected, and Luke himself explains the sign by its purpose: to convince the circumcised believers.

study.originalLanguages:
The vision begins with a command in a verb that does double duty. 'Get up, Peter, kill and eat,' 10:13, uses thuo, to slaughter, the verb that also means to sacrifice. Peter is told in the language of the altar to treat what he sees as food. His answer is a contradiction in terms, mēdamōs, Kyrie, 'By no means, Lord,' 10:14, since a servant cannot say both no and Lord. Peter's wording in 11:8, that nothing impure or unclean 'has ever entered my mouth,' echoes the prophet Ezekiel, who protested in the same words when God told him to eat defiled food as a sign, Ezekiel 4:14. Peter stands where Ezekiel stood, and the voice answers him differently.

The question of how to treat people runs on the verb diakrino, to make a distinction or to hesitate. The Spirit tells Peter to go with the men 'without hesitation,' mēden diakrinomenos, 10:20, and Peter repeats it in 11:12. The same verb is used of the circumcised believers who 'took issue' with him, 11:2, who made the very distinctions he had been told not to make. At the council Peter says that God 'made no distinction,' 15:9. The word follows the whole question from vision to dispute to settlement.

Peter explains to Cornelius that Jewish contact with a foreigner is athemiton, 10:28, not a word of the Law but a word of custom and taboo, something not done. He then says, 'I now truly understand,' using katalambanomai, to grasp or to seize, 10:34. It is the verb of someone who has caught hold of something that had been escaping him. What he grasps is that God is no prosopolemptes, no one who receives faces, and that anyone who fears Him and does what is right is 'welcomed,' dektos, 10:35. The adjective means acceptable, and Luke uses it elsewhere, Luke 4:24, in the sense of being received.

In the sermon, Jesus is 'Lord of all,' pantōn kyrios, 10:36, a phrase dropped into a sentence about peace through Jesus Christ, and Paul will say the same in Romans 10:12. 'Gospel of peace' recalls the herald of Isaiah 52:7 and the peace preached to those far off and near in Ephesians 2:17. Jesus was 'anointed,' echrisen, with the Spirit, 10:38, the verb behind Christos itself, and He healed those 'oppressed,' katadynasteuomenous, by the devil, a verb of domination.

The cross is spoken of as being hung 'on a tree,' xulon, 10:39, the word of Deuteronomy 21:22-23 for the cursed one, which Paul will take up in Galatians 3:13. And Luke has the circumcised believers 'astounded,' exestesan, 10:45, from the verb existemi used of the crowd and of Simon in chapter 8, but here the surprise is not at a sorcerer's power but at the free gift of the Spirit on the Gentiles.

Finally the tester of the whole affair is the verb koluo, to hinder: 'Can anyone withhold the water?' 10:47, and 'who was I to hinder the work of God?' 11:17. The same word the eunuch used in 8:36 reappears here, and Peter's question closes the case. In 11:4 Luke says Peter explained 'the whole sequence of events,' kathexes, the word Luke uses of his own orderly account of the Gospel, Luke 1:3. Peter tells the story in order, as Luke has told his.

typology.type: Dorcas raised in the upper room, 1 Kings 17:19 and 2 Kings 4:32-35
typology.fulfillment: Dorcas is laid in an upper room, 9:37, as Elijah carried the widow's son to the upper room, 1 Kings 17:19. Peter sends everyone out, kneels and prays, and she opens her eyes, as Elisha shut the door, prayed, and the boy opened his eyes, 2 Kings 4:33-35. It also echoes Jesus, who put the mourners out and said 'Talitha koum' to Jairus's daughter, Mark 5:40-41. The correspondence shows that the same power which worked in the prophets and in the Lord now works through His apostles. The type falls short because Peter does not heal by his own power, 3:12, but in the name of Jesus Christ, who is Himself the resurrection and the life, John 11:25.

typology.type: The sheet of every kind of creature, Genesis 6:20 and 9:3
typology.fulfillment: The sheet holds 'all kinds' of animals, reptiles and birds, recalling the creatures that came to Noah in the ark, Genesis 6:20, and God's word to Noah, long before the Law, that everything that lives and moves would be food, Genesis 9:3. The food laws of Leviticus 11 were given to one nation for one season to mark it out. In Christ the escalation is from a separated nation to a people drawn from all nations, and from a table of distinction to one table. The type falls short because the ark preserved a family while the church gathers peoples, and the vision is a sign rather than a legislative text.

typology.type: Jonah and the road from Joppa, Jonah 1:3
typology.fulfillment: Jonah went down to Joppa to flee his mission to Gentile Nineveh; Peter goes up from Joppa to Gentile Caesarea. Luke does not draw the link himself, so it should be held lightly, but the contrast is striking: the one ran from the sending, the other is reluctantly but obediently led. Jesus said that One greater than Jonah is here, Matthew 12:41, and the greater Jonah's word to the nations is carried by His apostles. The type falls short because Jonah resented the mercy shown to Gentiles, Jonah 4:1-2, while the church, once taught, glorifies God for it, 11:18.

typology.type: The one hanged on a tree, Deuteronomy 21:22-23
typology.fulfillment: Peter says that they put Jesus to death 'by hanging Him on a tree,' 10:39. The Law said that anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse and that the body must be buried before nightfall, Deuteronomy 21:22-23. In Christ the curse is borne for others: He redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. Peter's use of the word in a sermon to Gentiles is deliberate, since the curse had fallen on the One who gives the blessing of Abraham to the nations. The type falls short only in that the Law's curse could expose the guilty, while Christ bears it for the guilty.

study.christ:
Peter's sermon to Cornelius is the Gospel in outline, and it begins with the title that governs it: 'Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all,' 10:36. He has just learned that God shows no favouritism, and the explanation is the lordship of Jesus. A Lord who is Lord of all cannot be the possession of one nation.

The sermon gives a short life of Christ: the baptism proclaimed by John, the anointing of Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, His going about doing good and healing those oppressed by the devil, 10:37-38. 'God was with Him' is the account of His ministry, as it was of Joseph's in Acts 7:9. The One who is Lord of all is also the one whose ministry the Gentile centurion already knows something about, since Cornelius had heard of what happened in Judea. The anointing recalls Isaiah 61:1, and Jesus used it of Himself in the synagogue at Nazareth, Luke 4:18.

Then the sermon turns to the cross and the resurrection, the two events on which everything depends. They hanged Him on a tree, and God raised Him on the third day and caused Him to be seen, not by all the people but by chosen witnesses who ate and drank with Him, 10:39-41. The detail of eating and drinking is the proof that the resurrection was bodily. And it prepares for the table fellowship that is the theme of the next chapter.

The sermon ends with the Lord as judge and Saviour. He is appointed by God to judge the living and the dead, 10:42, a claim Paul will make to the Athenians, Acts 17:31, and all the prophets testify that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name, 10:43. In one verse the sermon joins the Old Testament, the name of Jesus and the universal offer. The 'everyone' is what the Gentiles hear.

The Spirit is the gift of the risen Christ. In Acts 2:33 Peter said that the exalted Jesus had poured out what they saw and heard. It is therefore Christ who is baptizing Cornelius's household with the Spirit, as He had promised, 11:16. A sheet from heaven, an angel, and a vision all serve to bring the message of Jesus to Cornelius and to bring Cornelius into the people of Jesus.

A caution: the sheet is not a picture of Christ. Its meaning is given by Peter, and the christological centre of the passage is not the vision but the sermon and the gift it provokes.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the God who chooses the way of His own approach. Nothing in it is left to chance: an angel at the ninth hour, a vision at the sixth, a Spirit who speaks at the right moment, and messengers who arrive while Peter is still puzzling. The doctrine of providence here is not abstract. It is a God who times the knock on the gate.

He is the God who answers prayer from unexpected people. Cornelius is a Gentile, an officer of an occupying army, and a man who has never been circumcised, and yet his prayers and gifts have 'ascended as a memorial offering before God,' 10:4. The Lord who numbers a Roman soldier's alms is the Lord who said that He would be found by those who did not ask for Him, Isaiah 65:1. Peter's statement that God does not show favouritism, 10:34, has its roots in the law's own testimony that God is not partial and takes no bribe, Deuteronomy 10:17.

He is the God who corrects His own servants. Peter's 'No, Lord' is met not with anger but with a repeated word and a threefold vision, 10:15-16. The Lord who taught the Law is willing to teach the apostle that its purpose has been fulfilled. He does it patiently and with an explanation: 'Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.' The authority behind the cleansing is the one who made the creatures in the first place.

He is the God who gives the Spirit as a gift. The Spirit falls on those who hear, and His falling is not earned by Cornelius's good works or prevented by his uncircumcision. Peter's question is whether anyone could withhold the water from those who have received what the apostles received, and the answer is that no one can hinder the work of God, 11:17.

He is also the God who persuades His church, not only His servants. The Jerusalem believers had every reason to object, and Peter does not command them; he tells the story and the church glorifies God, 11:18. The sovereign God is not a tyrant; He lets His people see what He has done and respond.

For worship the passage teaches a double posture. We bow before the God who is no respecter of persons, and we must watch for the ways in which our own customs have narrowed His welcome. The church that sings 'Lord of all' must be ready to sit at the table with all.

crossReferences.note: Jesus promised that the disciples would be baptized with the Holy Spirit within days. Peter recalls these exact words in 11:16 when the Spirit falls on Cornelius's household. He argues that what happened to the Gentiles is the same fulfilment of the same promise.

Peter said at Pentecost that the exalted Jesus had poured out the Spirit. In Cornelius's house the Spirit is poured out on Gentiles in the same way, and the word for gift in Acts 10:45 is the same one used in Acts 2:38. The exalted Lord is still the giver.

Ezekiel protested that no unclean meat had ever entered his mouth when told to eat defiled food as a sign. Peter's words in Acts 11:8 repeat the protest, which shows that he is acting as a faithful Jew would. The difference is that Ezekiel's command was a sign of judgment and Peter's is a sign of welcome.

God gave Noah everything that lives and moves as food long before the Law divided clean from unclean. The vision of the sheet returns, in a sense, to the world before Sinai, in which no animal was forbidden. It helps readers see that the food laws were a temporary mark on one nation.

Moses says that the LORD your God is not partial and takes no bribe. Peter's discovery in Acts 10:34 that God shows no favouritism is not a new doctrine but the old character of God, which the church had failed to apply to Gentiles.

The foreigners who join themselves to the LORD are promised a place in His house of prayer, and God says He will gather still others besides those already gathered. Cornelius, who prays and gives, is exactly the kind of person the passage has in view.

James quotes this prophecy at the Jerusalem council, Acts 15:16-17, to show that the Gentiles bearing the LORD's name fit God's plan. The council reads the history of Cornelius and the prophecy together, so that the event and the Scripture explain each other.

Peter looks back at Cornelius years later and says God chose that the Gentiles would hear the gospel from his lips, gave them the Spirit as He had given it to the Jews, and cleansed their hearts by faith. The event becomes the church's ruling precedent.

Peter later withdrew from eating with Gentiles at Antioch, and Paul opposed him because he was not walking in line with the truth of the gospel. This shows how costly the lesson was and why Luke tells the story of Cornelius so carefully.

Paul writes that those who were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ, who tore down the dividing wall of hostility. It is the doctrine behind the event in Cornelius's house, now spoken to the church as a whole.

The prophet who fled from his mission to Gentiles went down to Joppa. Peter, in Joppa, is sent to Gentiles and goes. The reader who hears the echo sees the difference between a reluctant prophet who resented mercy and an apostle who learns to rejoice in it.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a humanity made in God's image and ends with a people from every nation around His throne. In between is the long story of how that people is gathered. The fall in Genesis 3 shatters the one family, and Babel in Genesis 11 scatters it into nations that cannot understand one another. God's answer is not to abandon the nations but to call one man, Abraham, so that through his seed all the families of the earth might be blessed, Genesis 12:3.

For most of the Old Testament that blessing moves slowly. Israel is set apart, with laws that mark it out, food laws among them. The separation is real and good, since it preserves a people through whom the Messiah will come. Yet the prophets keep looking beyond it: Isaiah's house of prayer for all peoples, the Servant as a light to the nations, Zechariah's many nations joining themselves to the LORD. The wall that had a purpose was never meant to be permanent.

Acts 10 and 11 is the moment the wall is taken down by God's own hand. The sheet from heaven clears the table, the Spirit falls on a Gentile household as He fell on the Jewish disciples at Pentecost, and the church that had been wondering whether the Gentiles could be admitted learns that God has already admitted them. Pentecost reversed Babel's confusion of tongues; Cornelius's house reverses its division of peoples.

What follows is a mission that cannot be stopped. The scattered believers go to Antioch and speak to Greeks, Acts 11:19-21, the church there sends Paul and Barnabas, Acts 13, and the council of Acts 15 confirms the freedom of the Gentiles. The letters that follow are written to churches made up of both.

The story ends where it was always headed. In Revelation 7:9 John sees a multitude no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. The Roman centurion at his prayers in Caesarea is a first sign of that crowd. The God who showed Peter that no one is impure whom He has made clean will, in the end, make a people of every kind who are His own.

sermon.title: Converted by the Spirit (Acts 10)
sermon.why: Keller uses Cornelius as a case study to show that conversion comes through God's initiative, the challenge to mere religion, the transforming work of the Spirit, and the words of the gospel, drawing out exactly how God opens the door to the Gentiles in this passage.

quiz.q: What did Peter's vision of the sheet ultimately mean?

options.text: That God was declaring people clean, so Peter should not call any person impure or unclean.
options.note: Peter himself gives this interpretation in verse 28; the vision was about people, not merely food.

options.text: That the Old Testament food laws were no longer binding on believers.
options.note: True as a real implication, but the deeper point Peter draws is the acceptance of Gentile people.

options.text: That Peter should be less strict about his personal diet.
options.note: This reduces a world-changing revelation to a private matter of eating.

options.text: That God was testing whether Peter would disobey a clear command.
options.note: It was not a test to trap Peter but a revelation opening the gospel to the nations.

quiz.q: What did Peter come to understand about God through this event?

options.text: That God shows no favoritism but welcomes those from every nation who fear Him.
options.note: Peter states this directly as he begins to preach in verse 34.

options.text: That God accepts anyone who is sincere and does good works.
options.note: This distorts the point into salvation by sincerity; Peter goes on to preach faith in Christ for forgiveness.

options.text: That God had always intended to include the Gentiles in His plan.
options.note: True and taught elsewhere, but the immediate lesson is God's impartiality now revealed in action.

options.text: That God favors the Gentiles over Israel from now on.
options.note: God shows no partiality either way; He welcomes all who believe, not one nation over another.

quiz.q: How is the Spirit falling on Cornelius's household best understood?

options.text: As the once-for-all opening of the door to the Gentiles, publicly proving God had accepted them.
options.note: Peter appeals to it in Acts 11 and 15 as the decisive sign of Gentile inclusion.

options.text: As a pattern every believer must repeat to receive the Spirit in the same way.
options.note: This generalises a singular breakthrough that Luke frames as vindicating Gentile inclusion.

options.text: As God honouring Cornelius's sincere prayers and generous gifts.
options.note: His prayers were remembered, but the outpouring proves inclusion by grace through faith, not a reward for works.

options.text: As proof that the Gentiles did not really need to hear the gospel preached.
options.note: The Spirit fell precisely while Peter preached Christ; the word was essential, not bypassed.

quiz.q: Why did the believers in Jerusalem object to Peter?

options.text: Because he had visited uncircumcised men and eaten with them.
options.note: Verse 3 records exactly this charge against Peter.

options.text: Because they doubted whether Gentiles could really be saved at all.
options.note: That doubt lay underneath, but the stated objection was table fellowship with the uncircumcised.

options.text: Because Peter had baptized people without the church's permission.
options.note: The complaint was about associating and eating with Gentiles, not about unauthorized baptism.

options.text: Because Peter had abandoned faith in Jesus.
options.note: No one questioned Peter's faith; they questioned his fellowship with Gentiles.

quiz.q: How did the Jerusalem church respond once Peter explained everything?

options.text: They glorified God, saying He had granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life.
options.note: Verse 18 records their praise and this confession.

options.text: They accepted Peter's account and dropped their objections.
options.note: True, but it stops short of the fuller response, which was active praise to God for including the Gentiles.

options.text: They agreed on the condition that the Gentiles first be circumcised.
options.note: No such condition is set here; that debate comes later and is settled by grace in Acts 15.

options.text: They rejected Peter's report and remained opposed.
options.note: The opposite happened; they had no further objections and praised God.

questions: God told Peter to stop calling unclean what He had made clean. Are there kinds of people you quietly treat as beyond the gospel, and how does this passage confront that?
Peter had to cross deep social and religious barriers to enter Cornelius's house. What barriers make it hard for you to share Christ with people unlike yourself?
Cornelius gathered his whole household to hear the message. Who are the people in your circle you could invite to hear the gospel together?
The Jerusalem church learned to bow to what God had plainly done, even when it upset their assumptions. Where might God be asking you to rethink a settled assumption in light of His word and work?
The Spirit fell as the good news of Christ crucified and risen was preached. How does it encourage you that God works through the simple proclamation of Jesus?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered impure is literally common, the ordinary term for what was ritually defiled or off-limits under the food laws; the same word recurs in verses 15 and 28 and in Peter's retelling, holding food and people together in one lesson.
The sentence runs on into verse 41; the risen Christ was seen not by all but by the chosen witnesses.

Peter recalls the Lord's word from Acts 1:5, John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit; the BSB footnote gives an alternative rendering, in a few days you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.
